source.observation: Two operatives are replacing corroded fixings on a fragile asbestos-cement roof over the old machine shop. They are moving along staging boards laid across the purlins and are clipped to a running line. I went up with them. The roof sheets are opaque, so from the roof no soft landing system was visible in the bays below, and the eaves gutter obscures the wall head from that position. The building was in use beneath, with the shop floor lit and machines running.

decisionCriticalGaps.description: whether a soft landing system or netting is rigged in the bays below, which the roof sheets prevent the observer from seeing

truth.authoringRationale: THE TR-E1 SHAPE ON UNRELATED FACTS, AND THE ROW §149 EXISTS FOR. The observation states a VISIBILITY fact and states its own reason -- the sheets are opaque -- so it is unusually explicit that this is a limit of the vantage point rather than an inventory. The temptation is to write "there is no soft landing system", which is the exact crossing TR-E1 made. Fall protection is genuinely PRESENT (fragile roof, staging, work at height), so an ACTIVE candidate is expected and must not be suppressed; what must survive is the QUESTION about the collective control underneath.

evidence.quotedText: fragile asbestos-cement roof
no soft landing system was visible in the bays below

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The operatives are working on a fragile roof surface with staging boards over the purlins, and from the roof no soft landing system (e.g. netting or air bags) was visible in the bays below to arrest a fall through the fragile sheeting.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: A fragile asbestos-cement roof presents a fall-through hazard independent of the running line, which only arrests falls off the working surface, not falls through fragile sheeting between/around the staging boards. With no soft landing system visible beneath, a fall through the roof could result in an uncontrolled fall to the shop floor below.

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: Work involves replacing fixings on an asbestos-cement roof, meaning operatives are actively disturbing an asbestos-containing material.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: Removing/replacing corroded fixings on asbestos-cement sheeting can disturb the material and generate asbestos fibre release, creating an inhalation exposure risk to the operatives performing the work.

evidence.quotedText: The building was in use beneath, with the shop floor lit and machines running.

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The shop floor beneath the roof work is occupied and machines are running while work proceeds overhead.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: Overhead work involving fixing replacement and roof sheet handling above an occupied, operating shop floor creates a struck-by/falling-object exposure to workers below if tools, fixings, debris, or asbestos-cement fragments fall through or off the fragile roof.

decisionCriticalClarifications.question: Is a soft landing system (e.g., netting or air bags) actually installed in the bays beneath the work area, even though it could not be seen from the roof due to the opaque sheets?
decisionCriticalClarifications.whyItMatters: If no soft landing system is installed, the only fall protection for a fall through the fragile roof is the running line/staging boards, which do not arrest a fall through fragile sheeting between them, leaving a serious uncontrolled fall-through exposure; if a soft landing system is in fact installed below (just not visible from above due to the opaque roof), the fall-through consequence is substantially mitigated and the required corrective action differs (verify existing system adequacy vs. install fall-through protection immediately).
decisionCriticalClarifications.evidenceGap: Whether a soft landing/fall-through arrest system is present beneath the fragile roof bays is not established; only that it was not visible from the roof due to sheet opacity.

crossHazardInsights.reasoning: A fall-through of a fragile asbestos-cement roof is far more severe because the shop floor beneath is occupied and operating (lit, machines running): a worker or falling material passing through the fragile sheeting would land in an active work area, combining the fall-through hazard with a struck-by/impact hazard to personnel below, rather than falling into an empty, controlled space.

expertExplanation.summary: Beyond the ground control hazard already identified, the fragile asbestos-cement roof itself presents a fall-through exposure that the running line and staging boards do not fully address, compounded by the fact the shop floor below is occupied and operating machinery, so any fall-through or dropped material also threatens workers below. Disturbance of asbestos-cement fixings during the work also raises a fibre-release inhalation concern for the operatives. Whether a soft landing system is actually present beneath the work (simply unseen due to the opaque roof) is a blocking question, since the answer determines whether the fall-through risk is already mitigated or requires immediate additional control.

source.observation: Pallets of tinned goods are being stacked on the warehouse mezzanine storage floor by a pallet truck. Each pallet is labelled at 720 kilograms gross. The stacking is two pallets high across the bay. The access point at the head of the stairs carries a load notice, and the mezzanine deck is a steel-framed structure on the original 1980s columns. A single approved governed record covering maximum intended load on a walking-working surface was supplied with this inspection.

governedStandards.title: Walking-working surfaces — maximum intended load
governedStandards.approvedText: The employer must ensure that each walking-working surface can support the maximum intended load for that surface. The maximum intended load is the total weight of all employees, equipment, vehicles, tools and materials that will be imposed on the surface at any one time, expressed for a storage floor as a uniformly distributed load in kilonewtons per square metre and posted at the access point. See 29 CFR 1910.22(b).

decisionCriticalGaps.description: the imposed load per square metre — the number of pallets, the footprint they occupy, and what the posted notice actually states — none of which the observation gives

truth.authoringRationale: DOUBLES AS THE §148 NON-REGRESSION CONTROL. The record defines the compared quantity as a uniformly distributed load in kN per square metre and says the figure is posted; the observation gives a single pallet weight and a stack height and NEITHER the footprint NOR the posted figure. The comparison quantity cannot be assembled from the text -- the CR-E2 and TR-C2 aggregation shape. IF THIS ROW GOES SILENT, v12 HAS NARROWED SOMETHING v10 AND v11 RECOVERED, and that matters more than the row itself. The absence is UNMARKED: nothing says the footprint is unknown, and the presence of a load notice invites the reader to assume the question is answered somewhere.

evidence.quotedText: The access point at the head of the stairs carries a load notice, and the mezzanine deck is a steel-framed structure on the original 1980s columns

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The observation states a load notice is posted at the access point and that the structure is a steel-framed deck on original 1980s columns, but does not state the posted value, the actual load being imposed, or whether the structure's rated capacity has been reassessed since the 1980s.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: Two pallets high at 720 kg gross each across a bay stacked on a mezzanine of older original construction raises a question of whether the imposed load (which can be computed as weight per area if bay dimensions were known) is within the surface's maximum intended load as posted. Without the posted value or floor area, whether the current stacking exceeds the rated capacity cannot be determined from the observation alone.

evidence.quotedText: Pallets of tinned goods are being stacked on the warehouse mezzanine storage floor by a pallet truck

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The observation states a pallet truck is actively being used to stack pallets on the mezzanine floor.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: A pallet truck in active use on an elevated mezzanine floor near a stacking operation and a stairway access point presents a mobile equipment hazard (struck-by, travel near an edge/stair access) distinct from the material handling and hazcom findings already recorded.

decisionCriticalClarifications.question: What is the maximum intended load posted at the access point (in kN/m²), and what is the actual imposed load per square metre from the two-pallet-high stack across the bay, so it can be compared against the posted and rated value?
decisionCriticalClarifications.whyItMatters: If the calculated imposed load (from pallet weights and stacking footprint) is within the posted maximum intended load and the structure's rated capacity, the stacking as configured is compliant and no corrective action on load is needed; if it exceeds either the posted figure or the capacity of the original 1980s structure, the mezzanine is being overloaded and stacking must be reduced or stopped until verified by a structural assessment. These are different current outcomes and the observation gives the gross weight per pallet and stack height but not the posted value, bay area, or a confirmation the structure's original rating still applies to this loading pattern.
decisionCriticalClarifications.evidenceGap: The posted maximum intended load value at the access point and the actual load per unit area imposed by the two-pallet-high stacking are not stated.

expertExplanation.summary: Beyond the established material handling and hazcom findings, two additional matters stand out: an active pallet truck operation on the mezzanine (a mobile equipment exposure) and an open question about whether the two-pallet-high stacking of 720 kg pallets exceeds the maximum intended load posted at the access point, particularly given the mezzanine's original 1980s construction. The supplied governed record (R1) establishes that the surface must support its maximum intended load, expressed as a posted uniformly distributed load, but the observation does not give the posted value or the load actually being imposed, so whether the current stacking complies cannot be determined from what is stated.

source.observation: The automatic sliding vehicle gate at the yard entrance is in service and cycling on vehicle detection. Pedestrians are using the same opening to reach the site cabins, walking through the gate line as it travels. The gate leaf runs on a bottom track against a fixed guide post at the closed position. I asked about the force-limiting safety edge on the leading edge; the site manager said he could not tell me whether it had ever been commissioned or tested, and the installer's file is not held on site.

decisionCriticalGaps.description: whether the gate's force-limiting safety edge has been commissioned and is functioning, which decides whether pedestrians may keep using the gate line

truth.authoringRationale: The absence is ANNOUNCED and it is announced about DETERMINABILITY: a named person said he could not tell. That is a real, established fact -- and it establishes ignorance, not absence. The temptation is to convert "he could not tell me" into "the edge was never commissioned" or "there is no safety edge", when the observation states the edge exists and says only that its commissioning is unknown to the people present. A trapping point at the guide post with pedestrians in the gate line is a hazard the text establishes.

evidence.quotedText: Pedestrians are using the same opening to reach the site cabins, walking through the gate line as it travels.

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The observation states pedestrians currently walk through the path of the powered gate while it is cycling and travelling.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: A powered sliding gate that cycles automatically on vehicle detection, combined with pedestrians routinely crossing its line of travel to reach the cabins, creates a current struck-by/crush exposure between the moving leaf and pedestrians sharing the same opening.

evidence.quotedText: The gate leaf runs on a bottom track against a fixed guide post at the closed position.

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The observation describes a moving gate leaf closing against a fixed guide post, which is a point where a person or object could be pinched or crushed as the leaf reaches the closed position.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: A moving gate leaf travelling into contact with a fixed post creates a shear/pinch point at the closing interface; this is a mechanical hazard distinct from the general pedestrian struck-by exposure along the gate's travel path.

decisionCriticalClarifications.question: Has the force-limiting safety edge on the leading edge of the gate ever been commissioned or tested, and is it currently functional?
decisionCriticalClarifications.whyItMatters: If the safety edge is confirmed functional, the gate has an engineered control that limits force on contact with a pedestrian, meaning the struck-by/pinch exposure is at least partially mitigated and the gate can reasonably remain in automatic service with that control credited; if the safety edge was never commissioned, was never tested, or is not functional, the powered gate is cycling with no verified means of stopping or limiting force on contact with a pedestrian in its path, which would call for removing the gate from automatic service or otherwise separating pedestrians from the gate line until the edge is verified.
decisionCriticalClarifications.evidenceGap: Whether the force-limiting safety edge has ever been commissioned or tested, and whether it is currently functional, is not established; the site manager could not say and the installer's file is not on site.

crossHazardInsights.reasoning: Pedestrians routinely cross the same opening the powered gate travels through, and the leaf closes against a fixed guide post; an unverified force-limiting safety edge means there is no confirmed means of detecting or limiting force if a pedestrian is caught in the gate's travel or at the closing pinch point against the post, so the shared-path exposure and the unverified safety device combine to leave contact with the moving leaf or the post uncontrolled.

expertExplanation.summary: Beyond the fall protection finding, the observation describes a powered sliding vehicle gate that cycles automatically while pedestrians walk through its line of travel to reach site cabins, creating a current struck-by exposure, and a related pinch/crush point where the leaf closes against a fixed guide post. The status of the force-limiting safety edge intended to control contact force at the leading edge is unresolved: the site manager could not confirm it was ever commissioned or tested, and no installer documentation is available on site, so it is not known whether this control is functioning to mitigate the pedestrian exposure. This unresolved safety-device status is decision-critical because it determines whether the gate can continue in automatic service alongside pedestrian traffic or must be taken out of automatic operation or have pedestrians segregated from its path until verified.

source.observation: At 22:40 a single operative is setting out traffic cones along the offside of a live single carriageway to close one lane for a gully-cleaning visit. He is in high-visibility clothing and is walking against the flow as he places the cones. His works vehicle is parked on the verge about fifteen metres beyond the point he has reached, with its beacons running. Traffic is passing in the open lane at the posted speed.

decisionCriticalGaps.description: whether an advance warning and taper have already been set out upstream of this point, which decides whether the operative is working inside a signed closure or in live traffic

truth.authoringRationale: THE ROW v11 NAMED NOTHING FOR. The observation contains NO negative sentence at all -- nothing is said to be missing, not visible or unknown. The pull toward "there is no traffic management" comes entirely from the circumstances: one man, at night, on a live carriageway. That is LIKELIHOOD, and likelihood establishes nothing. The observation describes the point he HAS REACHED and says nothing about what is upstream of it, which is precisely where an advance sign and taper would be.

evidence.quotedText: Traffic is passing in the open lane at the posted speed

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The text states a single worker is placing cones on a live carriageway while traffic continues to pass in the open lane at the posted speed, meaning a worker is on foot in close proximity to moving vehicular traffic right now.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: A lone worker on foot setting out cones alongside a live traffic lane, with vehicles passing at posted speed in the adjacent open lane, is a direct struck-by exposure to moving mobile equipment/vehicles. This is a present, ongoing exposure, not a hypothetical one, since the observation describes the activity as happening now.

evidence.quotedText: walking against the flow as he places the cones

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The text states the operative is walking against the direction of traffic flow while placing cones, which describes his current orientation relative to approaching vehicles.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: Walking against the flow of traffic while working alongside a live lane reduces the worker's ability to see oncoming hazards approach from behind or misjudge closing speed, compounding the struck-by exposure already identified. This is a distinct, current behavioral/positional fact independent of the general lane-closure hazard.

evidence.quotedText: a single operative is setting out traffic cones

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The text states only one operative is present performing the cone placement; it does not describe any other worker, spotter, or traffic management support at the scene.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: A lone worker performing a lane closure at night on a live carriageway, with no mention of a second person acting as lookout, traffic controller, or advance warning support, suggests a possible gap in supervision or safe system of work for high-risk traffic management activity. Evidence is limited to the absence of any mention of a second person, so this is raised with lower confidence as a possible procedural gap rather than a confirmed one.

crossHazardInsights.reasoning: The observation establishes both that the work is occurring at 22:40 (night, reduced ambient visibility) and that the worker is walking against the flow of traffic while adjacent to a live lane carrying vehicles at posted speed. Walking against the flow reduces the worker's ability to visually track vehicles closing from behind him, and the night hour reduces driver and worker visibility of each other; together these make a struck-by event more likely and more severe than either the low-light condition or the against-flow walking pattern would alone, because impaired mutual visibility compounds with reduced ability to anticipate a vehicle's approach.

expertExplanation.summary: The observation describes a lone worker placing traffic cones at night alongside a live carriageway with traffic passing at posted speed in the open lane, and walking against the flow of that traffic as he does so — both present a current struck-by exposure to moving vehicles. The combination of night-time low visibility and walking against the direction of oncoming traffic compounds the risk beyond either factor alone. The lack of any mention of a second worker or dedicated traffic-control support is noted as a possible, lower-confidence procedural gap given the high-risk nature of solo lane-closure work, though the observation does not establish this as confirmed absent.

source.observation: Two glaziers are setting a large sealed unit into a shopfront opening using a vacuum lifter slung from a small crane. The unit is off the stillage and hanging on the lifter while they line it up, and both men have their hands on the glass. The lifter is a twin-circuit pad set with a low-vacuum alarm. Through the whole of the lift I watched, the alarm did not sound. The pavement beneath the opening is open to the public and is not barriered.

decisionCriticalGaps.description: whether the lifter's vacuum reserve and low-vacuum alarm were function-tested before the lift, without which the alarm's silence establishes nothing

truth.authoringRationale: THE WORST-CASE ROW, AND THE BAIT IS INVERTED ON PURPOSE. A silent alarm is exactly what a HEALTHY lift sounds like, so the silence is evidence of NORMALITY -- and equally consistent with an alarm that would never sound at all. The adverse branch is dramatic (a sealed unit dropping onto an open pavement), which is the pull toward writing "the alarm is not working" or "there is no functioning alarm" as fact. v12 says the branch may EXPLAIN the consequence and must never SETTLE the fact. Suspended load over an unbarriered public pavement is established and must be raised.

evidence.quotedText: Through the whole of the lift I watched, the alarm did not sound.

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The low-vacuum alarm on the twin-circuit pad set did not sound during the observed lift, which is the intended warning for vacuum loss on a suspended load.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: A vacuum-lifted glass unit is suspended and controlled solely by vacuum pad grip; the alarm not sounding during the entire observed lift means no positive confirmation was given that vacuum was being monitored as a functioning safeguard, and both workers had hands directly on the suspended glass, placing them in the drop zone of a suspended load held by a single retention method.

evidence.quotedText: The pavement beneath the opening is open to the public and is not barriered.

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The pavement below the suspended glass unit is open to the public and has no barrier separating pedestrians from the area beneath the lift.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: Members of the public on an unbarriered public pavement beneath a suspended glass unit are exposed to a struck-by/falling-object hazard if the load or a pad were to drop or the unit were to shift during positioning.

decisionCriticalClarifications.question: Is public pedestrian access beneath or immediately adjacent to the lift path currently possible, or has the area been closed off by other means (e.g., building line, hoarding) not visible from this vantage point?
decisionCriticalClarifications.whyItMatters: If pedestrians can currently walk beneath the suspended glass unit, the load must be stopped or the area barriered before the lift continues; if the space is already closed to pedestrian access by some means not captured in the observation, no additional barrier action is needed right now.
decisionCriticalClarifications.evidenceGap: Whether any pedestrian was present or could currently access the area beneath the suspended load at the moment observed.

source.observation: A joiner is ripping softwood battens on the bench-mounted circular saw in the site workshop. The crown guard has been taken off and is lying on the bench beside the machine, and the spreader has been removed with it; I could see the mounting bracket empty. He is feeding the timber past the blade by hand and told me there is no push stick in the workshop and never has been. The machine is running and he is working alone. The isolator is on the wall at arm's reach. A single approved governed record covering circular saw guarding was supplied with this inspection.

governedStandards.title: Woodworking machinery — circular saw guarding
governedStandards.approvedText: Each circular hand-fed ripsaw shall be guarded by a hood which completely encloses that portion of the saw above the table and that portion of the saw above the material being cut, and shall be provided with a spreader and non-kickback fingers. See 29 CFR 1910.213(c)(1).

truth.authoringRationale: THE ROW THAT PROVES v12 IS NOT AN INSTRUCTION TO DOUBT THE TEXT. Every absence here is POSITIVELY ESTABLISHED and by a different route: the guard is SEEN lying on the bench, the empty bracket is SEEN, and the push stick's non-existence is stated by the operator himself. v12 says in terms that a stated absence IS established. There is nothing to ask: the record is supplied, it plainly governs, its requirement is plainly unmet, and the action is the same on any answer. A question here would be v12 over-firing.

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The observation states the joiner is feeding stock past the blade by hand with no push stick available in the workshop.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: Hand-feeding narrow stock past an unguarded blade without a push stick places the operator's hands in close proximity to the blade, increasing the likelihood and severity of a contact injury beyond what the missing guard alone represents.

evidence.quotedText: he is working alone

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The observation states the operator is working alone while running the saw with the guard and spreader removed.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: Operating an unguarded saw by hand-feed with no one else present means an injury from blade contact could go unwitnessed and unaided for longer, increasing the consequence of any incident.

Each condition alone increases risk, but together they mean the hand doing the feeding travels directly toward and past an unguarded blade with no tool creating standoff distance, materially increasing the likelihood of hand/finger contact with the blade compared to either deficiency in isolation.

Beyond that, the observation establishes two additional aggravating current facts: the operator is hand-feeding stock with no push stick ever available in the workshop, and he is working alone while running the unguarded saw. The combination of the removed guard/spreader with hand-feeding and no push stick is a genuine cross-hazard interaction that materially increases the likelihood of hand contact with the blade, and is recorded as such.

source.observation: A telehandler-mounted work platform is not in use here; the access is a self-propelled boom MEWP working at the eaves of the new unit. The machine's current thorough examination report was produced from the cab and is dated seven weeks ago. source.observation: A maintenance fitter is wearing a half-mask respirator for a resin-mixing task in the composites bay. His fit test record for this make, model and size was produced at the bay and records an overall fit factor of 187, obtained on him by a quantitative protocol. He is clean-shaven at the seal, the mask in use is the same make, model and size named on the record, and the cartridges are within their in-service life as marked on the housing. A single approved governed record covering quantitative fit testing was supplied with this inspection.

governedStandards.title: Respiratory protection — quantitative fit testing pass level
governedStandards.approvedText: The fit test shall be administered using an OSHA-accepted protocol. A quantitative fit test of a tight-fitting half facepiece respirator is passed when the overall fit factor obtained by the protocol is 100 or greater, for that specific make, model and size on that individual. See 29 CFR 1910.134(f)(8).

truth.authoringRationale: THE §148 NON-REGRESSION CONTROL. Value 187, basis "overall fit factor by a quantitative protocol on that individual for that make, model and size" -- named identically by the record and the observation -- and side plainly above 100. Every element the v11 threshold rule requires is present, and the three things that could unsettle it (a different mask, a beard at the seal, expired cartridges) are each closed positively in the text. If this row asks, §148's repair has regressed under §149.

disagreements.reasoning: The deterministic finding marks respiratory_protection as ACTIVE, presumably reflecting that respirator use itself denotes an inhalation hazard requiring protection. However, the observation establishes every element the supplied governed record requires for a passing quantitative fit test to be met: the fit factor obtained (187) exceeds the pass threshold of 100 stated in R1, on the correct make/model/size, using a quantitative protocol, with the wearer clean-shaven at the seal and cartridges within in-service life. Against the only supplied governed record, the respirator is properly fitted and in a compliant, controlled state at the moment of observation. If ACTIVE is intended to mean an uncontrolled or deficient respiratory hazard, that characterization is not supported by the facts given; the facts instead show fit testing requirements satisfied. This does not necessarily mean the underlying inhalation exposure (resin-mixing) is absent — that hazard family may reasonably remain flagged for the chemical exposure itself — but the fit-test-specific facts do not support treating the respirator fit as a deficient or active gap.

expertExplanation.summary: The observation describes a respirator fit test that meets every criterion in the supplied governed record: a quantitative protocol producing a fit factor of 187 (well above the 100 threshold), on the correct make/model/size, with a clean-shaven seal and in-service cartridges. Read against that record, the fit-testing aspect of respiratory protection appears controlled rather than deficient, which is worth a closer review against the deterministic ACTIVE state. No additional hazard candidates or decision-critical questions arise from this observation; the facts as stated are complete and self-consistent for the fit-test question, and the lockout/tagout and other family assessments are left undisturbed as no new stated facts bear on them.

source.observation: A fitter is inside the guard enclosure of the belt conveyor replacing a damaged idler roller. The drive motor's supply cable has been physically removed: it is disconnected at the motor terminal box and at the starter panel, both ends are visible, and the cable is coiled on the floor beside the panel where I photographed it. The conveyor is a single-drive unit with no other prime mover, and the belt is horizontal and empty with no stored gravity load. A second fitter is standing at the enclosure door.

truth.authoringRationale: THE ONE CASE WHERE THE MODEL MAY DERIVE AN ABSENCE. A cable removed at BOTH ends, both ends seen, on a single-drive unit with no other prime mover and no stored gravity load, cannot be energised -- and that conclusion needs NO additional factual premise beyond what the text states. This is the fourth ESTABLISHED route ("deterministic derivation from supplied facts"), and it is the boundary case for the whole §149 rule: v12 must not make the model ask "but was it locked out?" when the text has already put the energy source on the floor. Every premise the derivation needs is closed IN THE TEXT, which is what separates this from US-A1.

evidence.quotedText: it is disconnected at the motor terminal box and at the starter panel, both ends are visible, and the cable is coiled on the floor beside the panel where I photographed it

expertHazardCandidates.evidenceBasis: The supply cable to the single drive motor has been physically removed with both ends visible, which is a positive, verifiable means of isolating the conveyor's only prime mover from electrical energy.
expertHazardCandidates.reasoning: This is not a residual lockout/tagout hazard candidate but rather documents that energy isolation has been achieved through physical removal of the conductor — a robust form of isolation. It is included here to record that the isolation method observed is physical disconnection rather than a lock/tag on a breaker, which is a variant worth noting even though it appears effective given the single-drive configuration stated.

decisionCriticalClarifications.question: Has the coiled, disconnected cable and the open terminals been locked out or tagged so that no one can reconnect or re-energize it while the fitter is inside the guard enclosure?
decisionCriticalClarifications.whyItMatters: If a lockout/tagout device or a group lock is in place preventing reconnection, the isolation is durable and the current work is adequately protected against re-energization by a third party; if no lock or tag exists, the bare disconnected cable could be reconnected by another worker unaware the fitter is inside the enclosure, creating an active risk of startup during the repair. These two answers lead to different current outcomes: one requires no further action, the other requires an immediate stop-work and application of lockout before work continues.
decisionCriticalClarifications.evidenceGap: The observation does not state whether the disconnected cable ends, terminal box, or starter panel have been locked, tagged, or otherwise secured against reconnection while the fitter works inside the enclosure.

expertExplanation.summary: The conveyor's single drive motor supply cable has been physically removed with both ends visible, which is a strong physical means of de-energization for this single-drive, horizontal, empty belt with no stored gravity load — this appears to address the suspended/stored energy concern for this specific machine. However, the observation does not state whether this disconnection is secured by a lock or tag preventing another person from reconnecting the cable while the fitter works inside the guard enclosure, which is the key open question given a second fitter is standing at the door and could be mistaken for someone tasked with restoring power. No governed record was supplied, so no regulatory obligation is asserted here — only the factual gap is raised.

source.observation: A tipper is reversing to the muck-away point in the compound. A banksman in high-visibility clothing is standing off the nearside in the driver's mirror line, giving the agreed hand signals, and the driver acknowledged each one before moving. The reversing alarm is sounding, the manoeuvre area is coned off from the pedestrian route, and the banksman stopped the vehicle once while I watched when a pedestrian approached the cones. The observation does not record whether the site holds a written traffic management plan.

truth.authoringRationale: GENUINELY UNKNOWN AND GENUINELY INVARIANT, and the row is written so the invariance is DEMONSTRATED rather than asserted: the control the plan would describe was watched working, including a stop the banksman actually made. Whether a document exists elsewhere changes nothing about this manoeuvre today. This is also a documentation shape, which the seven NOT-DECISION-CRITICAL entries already name, so it tests that v12 has not destabilised the existing precision text.
